description: We are a full team participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge with a focus on Mars mapping and interactive data visualization. Our four members come from aerospace, electrical, and computer engineering, and we study at SNU, KAIST, and DGIST. Each of us brings a different way of looking at the same problem. What brings us together is a simple goal: turning NASA’s planetary data into tools that people can actually use to explore, and maybe one day walk on, the surface of Mars.
summary:
Mars Mother is a web-based field exploration companion for the first astronauts to set foot on Mars. Our story begins where NASA’s Spirit rover stopped. Spirit kept exploring through a broken wheel and harsh Martian winters, and before it fell silent, the soil churned up by its dragging wheel revealed silica, evidence that hot water once existed there. Mars Mother lets an astronaut pick up Spirit’s mission on foot, across the same terrain, mapped with real HiRISE, MOLA and TES data and layers that highlight where signs of water are most likely to be found.

With no GPS on Mars, we adapted Censible, the global localization method JPL runs onboard the Perseverance rover, to match the terrain around the astronaut against orbital imagery and find their precise position. Routes are planned with D* Lite, weighing slope, sand traps, oxygen, radiation and return limits. When the ground turns out to differ from old maps, D* Lite repairs only the affected part of the plan, so the route updates in real time. A first-person AR HUD shows hazards, directions and live suit vitals.

Spirit’s own journey ended when it broke through a firm-looking crust into hidden soft sand, a reminder that on Mars, a single wrong step can end a mission. For an astronaut, it could cost far more than that. Mars Mother helps crews explore farther while always knowing they can make it back.
details:
1. Project overview

Mars Mother is a browser app built entirely from real mission data for Gusev Crater and the Columbia Hills, the region explored by NASA's Spirit rover. It combines a 2D map, a 3D globe, and a first-person AR-style HUD in a single app.

  • Target area: The area around Gusev Crater. The app provides a sampled 400 km × 400 km region around the crater and, for the central 30 km × 30 km in particular, high-resolution HiRISE DEM data and satellite imagery.
  • Target users: Astronauts exploring Mars, specifically those carrying out follow-up research to Spirit's search for traces of water.

Mars Mother was developed for two purposes.

  1. Supporting science exploration planning: For astronauts exploring Gusev Crater, it supports science exploration planning with a map that provides science layers, a range of geographic information, and real-time information.
  2. EVA navigation and situational awareness: It is a web-based navigation and situational awareness system for crew members performing EVA (extravehicular activity) on the Martian surface. It answers the three questions an astronaut on foot is constantly asking.
    • Where am I?
    • Where can I safely go?
    • Can I make it back?

2. How it works (1): Science and exploration tools

For the first purpose, supporting science exploration planning, the map provides four tools.

  • Science layers: These show geologic units, TES thermal inertia and sand-trap risk, aqueous and hydrous mineral detections, valley networks, and paleolake basins. All of them use JMARS datasets.
  • Point inspection: Clicking anywhere shows the coordinates, elevation, slope, temperature, radiation, atmospheric pressure, geology, and nearby minerals. A 360° view rendered on the fly from the DEM is provided as well.
  • Spirit's traverse: The rover's actual path, landmarks, and Pancam/Navcam photos are placed on the map as pinpoints, and the photos can also be viewed as panoramas. The route Spirit took in its search for water can serve as a reference for the current mission, and we expect it to be an important resource for a Spirit rover retrieval mission as well.
  • User pinpoints: Users can freely add and place pinpoints such as caves and bases. Base pinpoints are used to assess communication range and safety factors during EVA.

3. How it works (2): EVA navigation

The second purpose, EVA navigation, consists of four parts: localization, route replanning, physiology-based route costs, and environmental awareness.

Core feature 1: Finding your position without GPS

There is no GPS on Mars. So we implemented global localization by terrain matching, following Censible (Nash et al., ICRA 2024, NASA JPL), the method used on Perseverance.

  1. The surroundings seen from the ground are projected into a top-down view.
  2. A modified census transform is applied to both this image and the orbital map. This keeps the matching stable despite lighting differences between the ground and orbital views. Pixels with no data are not penalized.
  3. Hamming-distance template matching searches the uncertainty region around the estimated position.
  4. A sub-pixel refinement step yields the final position. A confidence score is also computed, based on how unique the match is.

We validated this feature with real data.

  • Demo mode: The actual 360° Navcam mosaic that Spirit took on sol 36 (NASA PDS) is matched against the HiRISE/CTX/HRSC orbital mosaic. The result is verified against the rover's true position, which we confirmed separately from the lander visible in orbital imagery.
  • Simulation mode: This works anywhere on the map. It degrades the orbital imagery by adding lighting changes, noise, stereo gaps, rock shadows, and heading error.
  • Step-by-step visualization: Each stage of the pipeline is visualized, so users can see for themselves why the system gave the answer it did.

Because photo data is available, even more precise navigation is possible.

Core feature 2: Routes that replan as Mars changes

Orbital maps were made years ago, and Mars keeps changing. Dunes migrate, slopes relax, rocks fall, and new craters form. So Mars Mother treats the map as a prior, not as ground truth.

  • In-situ surveying: As the astronaut walks, terrain within sensing range is "surveyed" and replaces the existing orbital data.
  • Incremental replanning: We implemented D* Lite (Koenig & Likhachev, 2002) from scratch. When the surveyed terrain differs from the map, it does not replan from the beginning. It updates only the affected cells and recomputes the remaining route from the current position in real time.
  • "True" terrain for the demo: This is generated by a simulated, seed-based terrain change model. The model includes DEM error, mass wasting (downslope movement of material), wind-driven sand transport, and local events such as new craters and rockfalls.

Routes computed for a human body

Routes are computed for a human body, not for a point on a map. Every edge of the route graph is costed with a physiological EVA model.

  • Walking speed: Tobler's hiking function, calibrated for a spacesuit.
  • Metabolic rate: The Pandolf load-carriage equation, adjusted for Mars gravity (0.378 g). The terrain coefficient is derived from TES thermal inertia, distinguishing firm ground from loose sand.

The app offers three routes.

- Safest route: Minimizes radiation exposure. It maintains line-of-sight (LOS) communication with the base, stays within range of a quick return, and avoids shadows, rough terrain, sand traps, and steep slopes.

- Shortest route: Prioritizes arriving by a short, fast path over other factors.

- Lowest-energy route: Computes metabolic rate with the Pandolf load-carriage equation adjusted for Mars gravity. It favors ground that is easy to walk on and has little slope over areas with many rocks or much sand.

Limits come from each crew member's profile (slope limit, oxygen tank, EVA duration, safety margin), so different astronauts may get different routes.

Environmental awareness

  • Mars time: The Mars24 algorithm (Allison & McEwen 2000) computes the sol date, season (Ls), and local true solar time.
  • Radiation: A surface GCR (galactic cosmic ray) dose model anchored to MSL RAD measurements. The value varies with elevation, seasonal and diurnal pressure cycles, the solar cycle, and terrain shielding.
  • Shadows: Terrain shadows are ray-traced from the actual position of the Sun at the selected time.
  • Communication: The line-of-sight communication range of the base antenna is computed, accounting for terrain and the curvature of Mars.
  • Point of no return: A map layer shows the boundary beyond which the remaining oxygen and time can no longer guarantee a safe return.
  • Sand and surface condition: Estimated using thermal inertia data.

4. Benefits

Mars Mother helps crew members on EVA make their own decisions in the field.

  • Position without GPS. It estimates the current position by terrain matching alone, with no satellite constellation.
  • Routes that fit the person. Routes account for the human body and consumables, and each astronaut gets a different route depending on their crew profile.
  • It copes when the map is wrong. If the actual ground differs from the map, the remaining route is recomputed from the current position in real time.
  • Earlier missions as a reference. Spirit's route can serve as a reference for the current mission and as a resource for a Spirit rover retrieval mission.
  • No heavy data to download. Multi-gigabyte GeoTIFFs are preprocessed into web assets, so users work directly in the browser without downloading large GeoTIFFs.

5. Intended impact

Mars Mother shows that a tool supporting crew decisions in the field can be built from publicly available NASA data alone.

Crew members on EVA have limited oxygen, limited time, and a long communication delay with Earth. Mars Mother estimates position without a satellite constellation, plans routes around the human body and consumables, and changes the plan when the actual ground differs from the map.

There are still few EVA-friendly Mars route-finding projects like this. We believe this program can become a stepping stone that directly helps not only the search for traces of water around Gusev Crater but also interplanetary exploration.

6. Tools and data

We used JavaScript as the language, VS Code as the IDE, and GitHub for collaboration.

- Front end: Built with plain JavaScript, HTML, and CSS, with no framework and no build step. The HUD uses three.js, and the globe uses CesiumJS with Cesium ion Mars 3D Tiles.

- Algorithm execution: All algorithms (D* Lite, census matching, and the EVA, radiation, and shadow models) run client-side in the browser.

- Data pipeline: Python (rasterio, NumPy, Pillow, Matplotlib) preprocesses multi-gigabyte GeoTIFFs into web assets. The outputs include files with 16-bit elevation values packed into PNG channels, image tiles, and GeoJSON. As a result, users do not need to download large, heavy GeoTIFFs.

- Accessibility: English/Korean switching, a responsive mobile layout, and an interactive onboarding tutorial.

The data we used:

  • HiRISE/CTX/HRSC DEM and visible mosaic of the Columbia Hills (~1 m/px)
  • MOLA+HRSC global DEM
  • NASA Mars Trek tiles
  • TES thermal inertia
  • JMARS science layers
  • MER-A traverse records
  • NASA PDS / Photojournal rover imagery

7. Creativity

Most Mars maps are made for scientists looking down from orbit. Ours is for a person standing on the surface.

  • We combined three fields into one tool. A rover localization technique from recent JPL research, an incremental path-planning algorithm from robotics, and a human physiology model from load-carriage research are brought together in a single tool for a person travelling on foot.
  • We started from the assumption that the map can be wrong. So the act of exploring itself updates the map, which improves the accuracy of the real-time route-finding algorithm.

8. Factors considered

  • Stating sources and assumptions: Every model cites its source. Assumed values, such as the spacesuit specifications taken from published Apollo A7LB and xEMU figures, are labelled as assumptions. Images rendered from terrain data are labelled as renderings, not photographs.
  • Validation with real data: Localization results were checked against Spirit's true position, and the traverse was checked against DEM landmarks. It matters that we actually validated what we built.
  • Ready for real hardware: The camera feed, heading sensor, positioning, and suit telemetry each sit behind their own interface. So a simulated device can be swapped directly for a real one. The HUD in the current demo is a simulation operated with a mouse and keyboard, but it is designed to be usable on Mars with only minor changes.
  • Human safety first: The absolute slope limit can never be overridden, and a safety margin is applied to every consumables budget.

References

  1. Nash, J., Dwight, Q., Saldyt, L., Wang, H., Myint, S., Ansar, A., & Verma, V. (2024). Censible: A Robust and Practical Global Localization Framework for Planetary Surface Missions. IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA). — localization
  2. Koenig, S., & Likhachev, M. (2002). D* Lite. Proceedings of the 18th AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence (AAAI-02), pp. 476–483. — route replanning
  3. Tobler, W. (1993). Three Presentations on Geographical Analysis and Modeling. NCGIA Technical Report 93-1, University of California, Santa Barbara. — walking speed
  4. Pandolf, K. B., Givoni, B., & Goldman, R. F. (1977). Predicting energy expenditure with loads while standing or walking very slowly. Journal of Applied Physiology, 43, 577–581. — metabolic rate
  5. Allison, M., & McEwen, M. (2000). A post-Pathfinder evaluation of areocentric solar coordinates with improved timing recipes for Mars seasonal/diurnal climate studies. Planetary and Space Science, 48, 215–235. doi:10.1016/S0032-0633(99)00092-6. — Mars time
  6. Hassler, D. M., Zeitlin, C., Wimmer-Schweingruber, R. F., et al. (2014). Mars' Surface Radiation Environment Measured with the Mars Science Laboratory's Curiosity Rover. Science, 343(6169), 1244797. doi:10.1126/science.1244797. — radiation
